comparator.name: Arts and Culture Studies
comparator.route: Arts and Culture Studies — standard domestic pathway
comparator.sourceNotes: Exact English-taught full-time BA specialisation, CROHO 56823, retained. The current official prospective year pages explicitly describe 2027–2028, 2028–2029 and 2029–2030: 60 EC first year; 30 EC second-year compulsory study and two 15-EC Faculty of Arts minors, one each semester; 20 EC third-year compulsory study, a 10-EC thesis and 30 EC free electives. The standard domestic third year appears first and is selected independently of UCR fit; it includes Conspiracy Culture, not the current older-cohort Adaptations component. The exchange pathway is a separate alternative, not added. The 2026–2027 OER confirms English ACS identity, academic aims and current conditions but its B2/B3 tables explicitly concern cohorts 2025/2024; it is not represented as the legal 2027 entrant curriculum. Known current prerequisites are Cultural Theory before Spatial Culture, Image Analysis before Visual Culture and compulsory B2 major courses before the thesis. All are compatible with this indicative sequence. Mentoring/PPO, RADAr and attendance are recorded separately. Current BSA is 45 of 60 EC. Earlier students who passed LET-ACWB708 replace the later festival course with a collective internship; this transition does not alter the new-entrant pathway. Future courses and regulations remain subject to change.
components: European Culture in a Global World
Two 15-EC Faculty of Arts minors, one per second-year semester; this is structured choice space, not unrestricted electives.
Required 10-EC bachelor thesis; current published progression requires completion of compulsory second-year major courses. Future regulations may change.

30 EC free-choice space. In the standard domestic pathway, 15 EC is taken in each semester; courses, internship and study abroad are possibilities subject to programme rules. The alternative exchange pathway is not added.

core: Analysis of art and culture across image, text, music, film, television, digital media and performance
Cultural theory, criticism, value and interpretation
Historical, social, political, global and identity contexts of culture
Cultural-studies research, critical writing, curating, festival practice and independent research
adjacent: Visual art, heritage, museums, material culture and curating
Literature, film, television, digital media and transmedial storytelling
Culture, identity, politics, inequality and power
Cultural criticism, exhibitions, festivals and public communication
questions: What counts as art, and how are cultural value and meaning assigned?
How do art and popular culture reflect and shape society, identity and power?
How do cultural forms travel across periods, media and geographical contexts?

trace: introduces visual and art-historical analysis across historical contexts
introduces close reading, literary interpretation and critical analysis of cultural texts
introduces film and media forms, histories and analytical concepts

Direct literary repertoire and interpretation: a chronological survey from Gilgamesh to postmodernity mainly addresses Western literary heritage and its cultural themes. Global breadth is supplied by World Myth & Literature and other courses, not attributed to this course alone.
examines how style produces meaning and develops precise critical writing
studies Renaissance art in connected Mediterranean and global historical contexts
develops qualitative research design, interpretation and reflexive analysis for cultural inquiry
provides historical analysis of political, social and cultural transformation
examines media histories, technologies and changing material forms
compares myth and literature across cultures, periods and media
introduces analysis of institutions, identities, inequality and social interaction
analyses how life and travel writing construct identity, place and intercultural encounters
examines documentary form, evidence, representation and creative non-fiction practice

Complementary ethical reasoning: moral theories, responsibility, equality and historical injustice support critical judgments about cultural institutions and representation; ethics is not a substitute for aesthetics.
examines African art and heritage through historical, social and postcolonial contexts
examines modern art, museums and institutions that shape cultural value and meaning
Direct media and cultural analysis: American racial histories, photographs, film and music examine systemic racism, representation, power and resistance; the final podcast is research-grounded.
studies relations between film and text, including adaptation and medium-specific meaning

Direct complementary theory of public culture: Gramsci, Habermas, Fraser, civil society, solidarity, the public sphere and decolonial critique support interpretation of cultural power. The empirical project studies a civil-society organisation, rather than a guaranteed arts institution.

Direct cultural theory and method: historiography from Vasari through Warburg, Panofsky, Gombrich, Foucault and Derrida examines aesthetics, authorship, identity and art-historical interpretation. No independent primary-research project is asserted.
examines competing theories and practices of literary meaning and interpretation

Direct creative-cultural analysis and practice: poetry, rhythm, voice, embodiment and hybrid projects connect interpretation with making. Music performance, singing and songwriting are expressly excluded; no festival-production or performing-arts qualification is claimed.

Complementary research method: students analyse diaries, letters, memoirs and official reports concerning the 1809 Walcheren Expedition and write a substantial paper. The military-history topic is fixed; this is not a freely chosen arts-and-culture thesis.
examines political authority, freedom, equality and competing justifications of power
Direct cultural and historical analysis: gendered American lives, storytelling, queer activism and cultural expressions are studied from the nineteenth century onward.
analyses how visual and audiovisual media construct environmental meaning across cultural and postcolonial contexts
examines empires, power, oppression and competing historical interpretations
analyses texts, films, exhibitions, protest art and social media in contested public debate
connects art, literature, architecture and heritage with democracy, inclusion and political participation

Complementary political-cultural context: theories of conflict consider ideology, identity-based grievances, colonial histories and justice/reconciliation across institutional and cultural perspectives; it is not an arts-analysis course.
uses feminist, anti-colonial and justice perspectives to study social movements and public action
examines emotion, experience and agency as dimensions of cultural meaning
develops rhetorical analysis, argument, writing and presentation for cultural criticism
studies material culture and identity across societies from a world-archaeological perspective

Complementary philosophical method: central questions about knowledge, reality, responsibility and freedom develop critical reasoning and argument. The enriched syllabus does not establish a dedicated aesthetics component.

Complementary public communication: framing, nudging, cognitive shortcuts and persuasion ethics develop analysis and application of influence in science, society and sustainability. The local-institution project is not guaranteed to concern arts organisations.

routeSelection.route: Arts and Culture Studies — standard domestic pathway
routeSelection.basis: The normalized target names the English-taught ACS specialisation; the official factsheet and OER distinguish it from Dutch ACW and Society, Language and Culture. Within ACS the standard domestic third-year curriculum appears before the exchange option and is the neutral choice. No named unverified track or selection for UCR fit is introduced.

selection.assessment: Three evidence-backed concepts respond to the defining analysis of art, cultural objects, interpretation and their historical and social contexts. The broad route combines artistic media; the second centres identity, representation and power with direct art, stylistics and adaptation replacing generic institutional politics; the third deepens text, screen and communication. Pairwise differences are 9, 5 and 12 courses. Curating and cultural-field practice remain evidenced, but the maximum of three is reached; no music, theatre or festival qualification is implied.

alternatives.label: Arts, media & cultural analysis
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum integrates art history and heritage, literature, film and media, philosophy, sociology, history, communication and qualitative and historical research.
alternatives.concept: A broad arts-and-culture route combining art history and heritage, literature, film and media with stylistics, social theory, ethics and qualitative inquiry. Historiography examines how art is interpreted; the historical research seminar studies a fixed military-history case rather than a freely chosen cultural-studies thesis.
progression: Introductions to art, literature, film, history and sociology support advanced museum, film-and-text, media-and-race and social-theory work. The Renaissance course is scheduled in its offered first-year spring; later historiography and literary-meaning courses are offered in final spring. All formal prerequisites are NONE; this does not turn course numbers into prerequisite rules.

alternatives.label: Culture, identity & power
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum centres cultural objects and interpretation, with historical, social and political analysis of identity and power.
alternatives.concept: A cultural-studies route examining identity and power through art, literature, media, gender history and heritage. Political philosophy, social theory, empire, social movements and conflict provide specific contexts; qualitative inquiry and a fixed-topic historical research seminar develop complementary methods.
alternatives.distinctness: Culture is organised around identity, representation and power through a sustained sequence of gender history, empire, heritage, social movements, political philosophy and conflict, alongside direct art, literary and media analysis. It differs from the preceding alternatives by [9] courses respectively; these differences follow the concepts and are not arbitrary threshold substitutions.
progression: History, political philosophy, sociology, gender, film and art foundations precede advanced social theory, media and race, film adaptation, ancient heritage and conflict. Introductory art history and film now precede the corresponding advanced work. All assigned terms are offered; formal prerequisites are NONE.

alternatives.label: Literature, film & cultural communication
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum forms a clear sequence in literature, film, media, rhetoric and creative communication, complemented by art history, archaeology, philosophy, history and qualitative research.
alternatives.concept: A literature, film and communication route organised around close reading, adaptation, documentary, rhetoric, stylistics and creative communication. Art history and material culture provide selected cultural contexts; general philosophy, ethics and qualitative methods contribute complementary analytical tools.
alternatives.distinctness: The programme shifts emphasis from broad visual-art and social-theory study to literary interpretation, adaptation, documentary and a 30-EC rhetoric, stylistics, persuasion and creative-communication sequence. Archaeology and philosophy supply specific complementary analytical contexts. It differs from the preceding alternatives by [5, 12] courses respectively; these differences follow the concepts and are not arbitrary threshold substitutions.
progression: Foundational literary, film and rhetorical work precedes advanced adaptation, literary interpretation, documentary and communication. General philosophy and qualitative inquiry support argument and research; no dedicated aesthetics syllabus is claimed. All formal prerequisites are NONE and all assigned offerings pass.

notes.text: The UCR programmes offer substantial art history, literature, film, media and cultural interpretation. Radboud additionally requires dedicated music analysis and music as technology, festival work and a separate bachelor thesis. UCR does not reproduce these specialist sequences. Its creative laboratory excludes music performance, and its history seminar studies the 1809 Walcheren Expedition.

audience.programmeDescription: The English-taught Arts and Culture Studies specialisation examines visual art, literature, music, film, television and performance through historical, theoretical and social perspectives. Students develop cultural criticism, research and cultural-sector practice.
audience.comparisonExplanation: Three UCR programmes offer related routes through arts and media, culture and power, or literature and communication. Radboud provides dedicated music study, festival production and a separate bachelor thesis. This comparison uses Radboud’s published indicative plan for students starting in 2027.
